section_title: Does calling something worship make it faithful to God?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Now a man named Micah from the hill country of Ephraim 2 said to his mother, “The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from you and about which I heard you utter a curse—I have the silver here with me; I took it.” Then his mother said, “Blessed be my son by the LORD!” 3 And when he had returned the eleven hundred shekels of silver to his mother, she said, “I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD for my son’s benefit, to make a graven image and a molten idol. Therefore I will now return it to you.” 4 So he returned the silver to his mother, and she took two hundred shekels of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a graven image and a molten idol. And they were placed in the house of Micah.

5 Now this man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and some household idols, and ordained one of his sons as his priest. 6 In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

7 And there was a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah who had been residing within the clan of Judah. 8 This man left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place. And as he traveled, he came to Micah’s house in the hill country of Ephraim. 9 “Where are you from?” Micah asked him. “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah,” he replied, “and I am on my way to settle wherever I can find a place.” 10 “Stay with me,” Micah said to him, “and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions.” So the Levite went in

11 and agreed to stay with him, and the young man became like a son to Micah. 12 Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house. 13 Then Micah said, “Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest.”

context_lines: The last five chapters turn from the accounts of individual judges to two extended stories of life within Israel. Here Micah, who lives in Ephraim’s hill country, admits taking eleven hundred shekels of silver from his mother. She has pronounced a curse over the theft; when he confesses, she blesses him in the LORD’s name.

After the money is returned, she dedicates it to the LORD for making images. Two hundred shekels go to the silversmith, and the images are placed in Micah’s house. He also makes an ephod and household idols, then appoints a son as priest. The word for household idols is תְּרָפִים, *teraphim* (teh-rah-FEEM). [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/8655.htm) identifies these as objects of reverence also used for seeking guidance; their exact appearance is not described here.

The narrator places this beside the statement that there is no king and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. The family uses the LORD’s name, but [Exodus 20:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/exodus/20.htm) forbids making and worshiping idols. [Deuteronomy 12:1–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/12.htm) directs Israel to the place God chooses, rather than leaving sacrificial worship to everyone’s preference.

A young Levite from Bethlehem arrives while looking for somewhere to settle. Micah offers him a yearly payment, clothing, and food to become his priest. The young man accepts and is treated like a son. Micah concludes that having a Levite guarantees the LORD’s favor. Yet [Numbers 18:1–7](https://biblehub.com/bsb/numbers/18.htm) distinguishes the wider tribe’s service from the priesthood entrusted to Aaron and his sons; hiring a Levite does not resolve the problems with this shrine.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-judges/) and [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/17.htm) both read the story as a warning about mixing religious language with disobedience. Wesley notes that the family means to honor the LORD by the images, rather than simply announcing allegiance to another god. Henry emphasizes how attachment to money leads into corrupted worship. Invoking God’s name does not remove the contradiction with His commands.

They also agree that Micah mistakes a favorable-looking circumstance for God’s approval. A Levite arriving at his door seems to him to confirm that the shrine will prosper. For these readers, his confidence exposes the problem: he treats one outward improvement as though it answers the deeper questions about whom and how he is worshiping.
god_plan_lines: The wider biblical story leads beyond Micah’s attempt to arrange access to God through a private shrine and hired priest. In [John 4:19–26](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/4.htm), Jesus speaks of the Father seeking worshipers who worship in spirit and truth. He also announces a coming change in the importance of the disputed places of worship and identifies Himself as the Messiah.

[Hebrews 7:23–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/7.htm) explains the lasting access God provides through Jesus: His priesthood continues because He lives forever, and He saves those who draw near to God through Him. The direction of the story is toward God providing the faithful priest and the way to approach Him, rather than people securing His favor by designing their own arrangements.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
